incidents.name: Dale Dyke Dam (Great Sheffield Flood)
incidents.cause_summary: The embankment failed during first filling; government inspectors pointed to design and construction defects in the puddle-clay core, though the exact initiating crack was never proven.
incidents.what_happened: The nearly completed earth embankment of Dale Dyke Reservoir at Bradfield failed as it was being filled for the first time, releasing roughly 3 million cubic metres of water down the Loxley valley into Sheffield. The flood destroyed mills, houses and bridges and inundated about 4,000 houses. Government inspectors later pointed to design and construction defects in the puddle-clay core, though the exact initiating crack was never proven.
incidents.status: historical / dam later rebuilt (1875); remains a landmark Victorian civil-engineering disaster
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: thousands of households flooded; 600+ houses damaged or destroyed
incidents.notes: Chief Constable recorded 240 deaths; later local research suggests additional indirect deaths not on the official list.
incidents.volume_released: roughly 3 million cubic metres
incidents.downstream_risk: Loxley valley and Sheffield; about 4,000 houses inundated
incidents.economic_damage: claims raised over £42,000 in contemporary relief; one of the largest Victorian insurance claims
incidents.investigating_agency: Home Office inquiry (Robert Rawlinson and Nathaniel Beardmore)

incidents.name: Williamsburg Reservoir Dam (Mill River Flood)
incidents.geo_source: Historic Dam Trail / 3 mi north of Williamsburg center
incidents.cause_summary: A poorly constructed earthen reservoir dam failed; the Hampshire County coroner's jury found fault with the reservoir company, engineers, contractors and weak state regulation.
incidents.what_happened: A poorly constructed earthen reservoir dam on the Mill River above Williamsburg, Massachusetts, failed and sent a flood wave through Williamsburg, Skinnerville, Haydenville and Leeds. The Hampshire County coroner's jury found fault with the reservoir company, engineers, contractors and weak state regulation. It was the deadliest U.S. dam failure until Johnstown in 1889.
incidents.status: historical / not rebuilt as a high dam; documented ASDSO case study
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: four mill villages wrecked along a narrow valley
incidents.notes: Town vital records and contemporary newspapers document 139 deaths, including 43 children under 10.
incidents.volume_released: about 600 million gallons
incidents.breach_size: about 250 ft-wide breach in the ~600 ft dam
incidents.downstream_risk: Williamsburg, Skinnerville, Haydenville and Leeds mill villages

incidents.name: South Fork Dam (Johnstown Flood)
incidents.river_or_facility: South Fork Little Conemaugh River / Lake Conemaugh
incidents.cause_summary: After days of heavy rain the earthfill dam overtopped and failed, after modifications that lowered the crest, clogged the spillway with fish screens and removed discharge pipes.
incidents.what_happened: After days of heavy rain, the earthfill South Fork Dam owned by the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club overtopped and failed at about 15:15, releasing Lake Conemaugh toward Johnstown. Modifications that lowered the crest, clogged the spillway with fish screens and removed discharge pipes reduced freeboard and outlet capacity. The debris-laden wave destroyed towns along the Little Conemaugh and burned at the Stone Bridge in Johnstown.
incidents.status: historical / Johnstown Flood National Memorial at the dam site
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 1,600 homes lost; Johnstown and upstream valley towns destroyed
incidents.notes: NPS and Rev. David J. Beale’s contemporary catalogue give 2,209 deaths, the standard official figure.
incidents.owner_operator: South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club
incidents.reservoir_capacity: about 480 million cubic feet (original Western Reservoir)
incidents.volume_released: Lake Conemaugh (about 20 million tons of water)
incidents.downstream_risk: Johnstown and towns along the Little Conemaugh
incidents.economic_damage: $17 million (1889)

incidents.name: Austin (Bayless) Dam
incidents.cause_summary: Investigators found sliding on a faulty foundation plus design, construction and operation defects.
incidents.what_happened: The concrete gravity Bayless Dam above Austin, Pennsylvania, collapsed after less than two years of troubled service, releasing a flood that destroyed Austin and Costello. Investigators found sliding on a faulty foundation plus design, construction and operation defects. The disaster helped produce Pennsylvania’s 1913 dam-safety law.
incidents.status: historical / a later rebuilt dam also failed in 1942 without deaths; ruins remain
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: towns of Austin and Costello largely destroyed
incidents.notes: Confirmed deaths are 78; some contemporary reports were higher because of unrecorded itinerant workers.
incidents.breach_size: part of the 540 ft dam slid about 50 ft; another section opened like a door
incidents.downstream_risk: Austin and Costello
incidents.economic_damage: roughly $10 million property damage
incidents.investigating_agency: State Conservation Commission / investigators of the 1911 failure

incidents.name: Gleno Dam
incidents.cause_summary: The dam failed about 40 days after first full filling; investigations blamed structural deficiencies, poor construction and cost-cutting.
incidents.what_happened: A multiple-arch buttress dam completed in 1923 failed about 40 days after first full filling, releasing about 4.5 million cubic metres of water. The flood destroyed or damaged Bueggio, Dezzo and Corna di Darfo before reaching Lake Iseo. Investigations blamed structural deficiencies, poor construction and cost-cutting. It reshaped Italian dam regulation.
incidents.status: historical / surviving ruined structure still stands; not returned to service
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: several Alpine villages destroyed or flooded
incidents.notes: Academic accounts use at least 356; some local histories cite 359 confirmed or estimates up to about 500.
incidents.volume_released: about 4.5 million cubic metres
incidents.breach_size: middle section collapsed
incidents.downstream_risk: Bueggio, Dezzo, Corna di Darfo and other Alpine villages

incidents.name: Eigiau and Coedty Dams (Dolgarrog disaster)
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (Llyn Eigiau; first dam to fail)
incidents.river_or_facility: Llyn Eigiau / Coedty / Afon Porth Llŵyd
incidents.cause_summary: The Eigiau concrete dam failed on poor glacial foundations after autumn rains, sending water into the lower Coedty embankment, which then failed.
incidents.what_happened: The concrete dam at Llyn Eigiau failed on poor glacial foundations after autumn rains, sending water into the lower Coedty embankment, which then failed. The combined flood and boulder debris destroyed part of Dolgarrog. The disaster led to the Reservoirs (Safety Provisions) Act 1930, the UK’s first dam-safety statute.
incidents.status: historical / Eigiau not rebuilt as a high dam; Coedty later rebuilt
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: northern Dolgarrog and Porth Llŵyd settlement destroyed
incidents.notes: Memorial and contemporary accounts name 16 dead (10 adults, 6 children).
incidents.volume_released: combined Eigiau and Coedty reservoirs
incidents.downstream_risk: northern Dolgarrog and Porth Llŵyd

incidents.name: St. Francis Dam
incidents.location_label: San Francisquito Canyon, California, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: San Francisquito Canyon / Santa Clara River
incidents.cause_summary: Foundation and design flaws, including weak rock and a known fault, are the accepted causes of the collapse after the reservoir had been filled to capacity.
incidents.what_happened: The concrete gravity-arch St. Francis Dam, part of the Los Angeles aqueduct system, collapsed just before midnight after the reservoir had been filled to capacity. A flood of about 12 billion gallons swept 54 miles down the Santa Clara River valley to the Pacific. Foundation and design flaws, including weak rock and a known fault, are the accepted causes.
incidents.status: historical / not rebuilt; California Historic Landmark
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 1,000+ houses damaged or destroyed along the Santa Clara valley

incidents.downstream_risk: San Francisquito Canyon and Santa Clara River valley to the Pacific; 1,000+ houses damaged or destroyed

incidents.name: Vega de Tera Dam (Ribadelago)
incidents.river_or_facility: Tera River / Vega de Tera reservoir
incidents.cause_summary: A section of the buttress dam collapsed; poor construction quality and materials were identified.
incidents.what_happened: A section of the Vega de Tera buttress dam collapsed around midnight, releasing about 7.8 million cubic metres of water. The flood reached Ribadelago in minutes, destroying most of the village and sweeping victims into Lake Sanabria. Poor construction quality and materials were identified. Convictions of company officials were later overturned or pardoned under the Franco regime.

incidents.name: Malpasset Dam
incidents.cause_summary: The arch dam failed during first complete filling after heavy rain; post-failure studies attributed the collapse to foundation uplift on a faulted micaschist abutment.
incidents.what_happened: The thin Malpasset arch dam failed suddenly at about 21:11 during first complete filling after heavy rain, releasing about 50 million cubic metres of water down the Reyran valley. Fréjus was inundated within about 21 minutes. Post-failure studies attributed the collapse to foundation uplift on a faulted micaschist abutment. Courts did not assign criminal liability to the builders.
incidents.status: historical / dam not rebuilt; ruins remain a major ICOLD/ARIA case study
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 7,000 homeless
incidents.notes: Most French official sources use 423 deaths; some ARIA pages say 421.
incidents.volume_released: about 50 million cubic metres
incidents.breach_size: arch dam failed suddenly
incidents.downstream_risk: Fréjus; about 7,000 homeless
incidents.economic_damage: equivalent of about US$68 million

incidents.name: Panshet and Khadakwasla Dams
incidents.cause_summary: Unfinished Panshet failed after outlet-conduit problems and first-filling stresses; the flood then overtopped and breached older masonry Khadakwasla downstream.
incidents.what_happened: The unfinished earthen Panshet Dam failed in the early hours of 12 July 1961 after outlet-conduit problems and first-filling stresses. The flood wave then overtopped and breached the older masonry Khadakwasla Dam downstream. Central Pune was inundated; Khadakwasla’s temporary resistance after dawn allowed many residents to move to higher ground. The event remains the city’s defining flood disaster.
incidents.status: historical / both dams later rebuilt; Pune floodplain planning still references 1961
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: tens of thousands homeless; over 100,000 homes reported damaged in later summaries
incidents.notes: Widely cited figure is about 1,000 deaths. Some unofficial estimates are higher; a precise official register is not consistently published.
incidents.reservoir_capacity: Panshet planned 7.54 TMC; Khadakwasla about 2 TMC
incidents.breach_size: about 30-ft area near the slipway gave way before the wall failed
incidents.downstream_risk: central Pune; tens of thousands homeless

incidents.name: Vajont Dam landslide and overtopping
incidents.location_label: Longarone / Erto e Casso, Veneto–Friuli, Italy
incidents.cause_summary: During first filling a landslide from Monte Toc entered the reservoir and generated a wave that overtopped the intact dam wall, destroying Longarone and nearby villages.
incidents.what_happened: During first filling, a roughly 260-million-cubic-metre landslide from Monte Toc entered the Vajont reservoir at 22:39, generating a wave that overtopped the dam by about 250 m. About 50 million cubic metres of water destroyed Longarone and nearby villages in minutes. The concrete arch dam itself remained essentially intact. Official data speak of 1,917 victims; higher estimates exist because many bodies were never identified.
incidents.status: historical / dam still standing, reservoir filled with landslide debris, not in operation
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Longarone, Pirago, Rivalta, Villanova, Faè and lakeside hamlets destroyed

incidents.volume_released: about 50 million cubic metres overtopped the dam

incidents.downstream_risk: Longarone, Pirago, Rivalta, Villanova, Faè and lakeside hamlets
incidents.investigating_agency: Italian criminal courts / Ministry of Public Works inquiries

incidents.name: Baldwin Hills Dam
incidents.cause_summary: Investigations linked the breach to foundation displacement along the Newport–Inglewood fault system, with oil-field operations later the subject of civil settlement.
incidents.what_happened: A caretaker noticed lining leakage on the morning of 14 December 1963; police evacuated about 1,600 people before the Baldwin Hills Reservoir dam breached at 15:38. About 250–290 million gallons flooded a square mile of South Los Angeles, destroying or damaging 277 homes. Investigations linked the breach to foundation displacement along the Newport–Inglewood fault system, with oil-field operations later the subject of civil settlement.
incidents.status: historical / reservoir not rebuilt; site is now Kenneth Hahn State Recreation Area
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 1,600 evacuated; 277 homes destroyed or damaged
incidents.notes: Five named fatalities. Early detection and evacuation are credited with preventing a far larger death toll.
incidents.owner_operator: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
incidents.volume_released: about 250–290 million gallons
incidents.downstream_risk: South Los Angeles neighbourhoods; about 1,600 evacuated; 277 homes destroyed or damaged

incidents.name: Swift and Two Medicine Dams (Blackfeet Flood)
incidents.location_label: Blackfeet Indian Reservation, Montana, United States
incidents.cause_summary: A rain-on-snow storm produced extreme runoff; Swift Dam failed and additional Reservation deaths were attributed to extreme spillway discharge at Lower Two Medicine Dam.
incidents.what_happened: A rain-on-snow storm in early June 1964 produced extreme runoff across northwestern Montana. Swift Dam failed about 10:10 on 8 June, killing 19 people on the Blackfeet Reservation. Lower Two Medicine Dam also failed; nine additional Reservation deaths were attributed to extreme spillway discharge before that failure. USGS documented the flood; Gibson Dam overtopped but held.
incidents.status: historical / both failed dams later addressed; statewide flood remains a USGS reference storm
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 8,700 evacuated statewide during the high-water period
incidents.notes: Deaths: 19 from Swift failure + 9 associated with Two Medicine spillway flooding (USGS/ASDSO). Statewide flood deaths were 30.

incidents.downstream_risk: Blackfeet Reservation communities along Birch Creek and Two Medicine Creek
incidents.economic_damage: statewide flood damages over $500 million in 2020 dollars

incidents.name: El Cobre tailings dams (El Soldado)
incidents.cause_summary: The 28 March 1965 La Ligua / Valparaíso earthquake liquefied hydraulic-fill tailings dams at El Soldado, releasing about 2 million cubic metres of tailings.
incidents.what_happened: The 28 March 1965 La Ligua / Valparaíso earthquake liquefied hydraulic-fill tailings dams at the El Soldado copper mine. Two dams released on the order of 2 million cubic metres of tailings that travelled about 12 km and buried the town of El Cobre. The event drove Chilean abandonment of upstream tailings construction in seismic areas and helped motivate a national emergency office.
incidents.status: historical / town not rebuilt on the same site; major global tailings-seismic case
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: El Cobre buried; 60–70 farmhouses swept away
incidents.notes: Official death toll 247; incomplete camp records lead many sources to estimate 350–400.

incidents.volume_released: on the order of 2 million cubic metres of tailings
incidents.downstream_risk: El Cobre buried; 60–70 farmhouses swept away

incidents.name: Aberfan colliery spoil tip (Tip 7)
incidents.location_label: Aberfan, Merthyr Tydfil, Wales, United Kingdom
incidents.river_or_facility: Merthyr Vale Colliery spoil tips above Aberfan
incidents.cause_summary: Colliery spoil Tip 7, built over springs, liquefied after heavy rain and slid into Aberfan; the official tribunal placed blame on the National Coal Board.
incidents.what_happened: Colliery spoil Tip 7, built over springs on the hillside above Aberfan, liquefied after heavy rain and slid into the village on 21 October 1966. The flow engulfed Pantglas Junior School and nearby houses. The official tribunal placed blame on the National Coal Board. This is a coal-spoil tip, not a water-retaining dam, included as tailings-adjacent because the mechanism (liquefied mining waste) is the same class of failure.
incidents.status: historical / tips removed or remediated; Aberfan Disaster Tribunal is the authoritative record
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Pantglas Junior School and 18 houses destroyed
incidents.notes: Official toll 144 (116 children, 28 adults). Type recorded as tailings with an explicit tip/colliery-spoil note.

incidents.name: Buffalo Creek coal-waste dams
incidents.location_label: Logan County, West Virginia, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Middle Fork of Buffalo Creek (Pittston / Buffalo Mining)
incidents.cause_summary: A coal-refuse impoundment failed after rain; state and federal inquiries found improper construction, while the company called it an act of God.

State and federal inquiries found improper construction; the company called it an act of God. The disaster drove federal coal-refuse impoundment regulation.

incidents.name: Canyon Lake Dam (Black Hills / Rapid City flood)
incidents.location_label: Rapid City, South Dakota, United States
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (1972 Black Hills flood / Canyon Lake)
incidents.cause_summary: Extreme thunderstorms dumped more than 10–15 inches of rain; debris clogged the spillway and the dam overtopped and failed about 22:45.
incidents.what_happened: Extreme thunderstorms dumped more than 10–15 inches of rain on the Black Hills on 9–10 June 1972. Debris clogged the Canyon Lake Dam spillway; the dam overtopped and failed about 22:45. USGS concluded that most of Rapid City’s peak flow came from rainfall downstream of Pactola Dam rather than Canyon Lake storage, but the breach sent a surge into the city. The flood is among the deadliest in U.S. history.

incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 1,335 homes destroyed; 5,000 automobiles destroyed

incidents.name: Banqiao and Shimantan Dams (Typhoon Nina)
incidents.cause_summary: After Typhoon Nina stalled over the Huai basin, Banqiao Dam breached and Shimantan and dozens of other dams failed in a cascade.
incidents.what_happened: After Typhoon Nina stalled over the Huai basin, Banqiao Dam breached about 01:00 on 8 August 1975 and Shimantan and dozens of other dams failed in a cascade. Official accounts describe about 6 billion cubic metres of floodwater over some 10,000 km². Daowencheng commune was wiped out. incidents.name: Rishiganga and Tapovan hydropower works (Chamoli flood)
incidents.cause_summary: A rock-and-ice avalanche from Ronti Peak generated a debris flood that destroyed the hydropower works; the record states this was not a classic overtopping or piping failure.
incidents.what_happened: A rock-and-ice avalanche from Ronti Peak on 7 February 2021 generated a debris flood that washed away the 13.2 MW Rishiganga project and heavily damaged NTPC’s under-construction Tapovan Vishnugad works, trapping labourers in a tunnel. This was destruction of dams by an extreme geomorphic flood, not a classic overtopping or piping failure. Most victims were project workers. By May 2021 authorities had recovered 83 bodies and 36 body parts from 204 people listed missing.
incidents.status: historical / projects destroyed or severely damaged; Himalayan cascade-hydropower risk case
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Raini/Lata area and 13 villages cut off when a bridge washed out; 204 listed missing at peak
incidents.notes: Deaths field uses recovered bodies (83 as of May 2021). Combined dead and missing is about 200. Not a structural dam-break; included because both hydropower dams were destroyed.
incidents.year_built: Tapovan under construction; Rishiganga 13.2 MW project in service
incidents.downstream_risk: Raini/Lata area and 13 villages cut off; most victims were project workers

incidents.name: Jagersfontein tailings dam
incidents.cause_summary: A diamond-tailings dam failed, releasing more than 6 million m³ of sludge; the record does not state an established failure mechanism.
incidents.what_happened: A diamond-tailings dam at Jagersfontein failed about 06:00 on 11 September 2022, releasing more than 6 million m³ of sludge that destroyed houses and about 1,600 ha of land. The facility had been shut in 2020 over high water levels and allowed to resume in 2021. Provincial officials confirmed one death and about 40 injured; two people were later still listed missing. Academic reconstruction cites two dead and one missing.
incidents.status: historical / operations halted; highlighted patchy tailings regulation in South Africa
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: nearly 200 houses smothered; 160+ residents displaced
incidents.notes: Official confirmed death toll remained 1 (Mr Mosweu) with two missing in late September 2022. A 2024 academic paper states two died and one remained missing.
incidents.volume_released: more than 6 million m³ of sludge
incidents.downstream_risk: nearly 200 houses smothered; 160+ residents displaced; about 1,600 ha of land

incidents.name: Kakhovka Dam
incidents.cause_summary: The dam was destroyed during the Russia–Ukraine war; responsibility for the blast remains contested, and the record treats it as wartime destruction rather than a peacetime engineering failure.
incidents.what_happened: The Kakhovka Dam was destroyed in the early hours of 6 June 2023 during the Russia–Ukraine war, releasing more than 14–18 km³ of reservoir water. Downstream communities in Kherson and Mykolaiv oblasts flooded on both banks; upstream areas lost water supply. A UN-supported PDNA for government-controlled areas recorded 31 dead, 28 injured and 41 missing as of 17 July, with 2,783 evacuated. Russian-installed officials separately reported 59 deaths. Responsibility for the blast remains contested.
incidents.status: historical / dam and hydropower plant destroyed; reservoir largely emptied; reconstruction not complete as of 2026
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: ~100,000 residents directly impacted; up to 1 million lost drinking-water access
incidents.notes: Deaths field uses Ukrainian/PDNA figure of 31 in government-controlled areas. Russian-installed authorities reported 59. Local accounts from occupied Oleshky alleged hundreds. Cause: wartime destruction, not a peacetime engineering failure.
incidents.volume_released: more than 14–18 km³ of reservoir water
incidents.breach_size: dam and hydropower plant destroyed
incidents.downstream_risk: ~100,000 residents directly impacted; up to 1 million lost drinking-water access
incidents.economic_damage: Ukrhydroenergo said rebuilding would take at least five years and $1 billion

incidents.name: Abu Mansur (Bu Mansour) and Derna / Al-Bilad Dams
incidents.cause_summary: Storm Daniel dropped extreme rain that failed the two 1970s dams in cascade; the record states the dams had documented maintenance neglect.
incidents.what_happened: Storm Daniel dropped extreme rain on northeastern Libya on 10 September 2023. The upstream 75 m Abu Mansur dam failed first, then the downstream Derna (Al-Bilad) dam, releasing on the order of 30 million cubic metres through the city of Derna. The 1970s Yugoslav-built dams had documented maintenance neglect. WMO said most deaths were avoidable with warnings. Official Libyan figures later cited 4,540 dead and 3,297 missing; earlier Red Crescent/UN figures exceeded 11,000.
incidents.status: historical / Derna partly destroyed; investigations into maintenance funds and warnings ongoing
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: large part of Derna destroyed; thousands of buildings damaged
incidents.notes: Deaths field uses later official government figure 4,540. WHO/OCHA later cited about 3,958. Libyan Red Crescent briefly 11,300. Mayor speculated 18,000–20,000. Second-deadliest dam disaster after Banqiao on most rankings.
incidents.owner_operator: Libyan state (built by Yugoslav firm Hidroprojekt / Hidroprojekat)
incidents.reservoir_capacity: Abu Mansur about 18–23.7 million m³; Al-Bilad about 1.2–1.5 million m³
incidents.volume_released: on the order of 30 million cubic metres
incidents.downstream_risk: city of Derna; large part of the city destroyed
incidents.investigating_agency: Libyan investigations into maintenance funds and warnings

incidents.name: Gedzhukh (Gejukh) Reservoir dam
incidents.cause_summary: After extreme Caspian-cyclone rainfall the earthen dam gave way; a criminal case was opened over maintenance, and prosecutors said the operator had not ensured safe operation.
incidents.what_happened: After extreme Caspian-cyclone rainfall, the earthen dam of the Gedzhukh (Gejukh) Reservoir in Derbent District gave way on 5 April 2026 (RIA Novosti; some later court/investigative copy says 6 April). Water hit Mamedkala and nearby settlements including Yuny Pakhar, Gejuk and Kala. RIA, quoting Head of Dagestan Sergey Melikov, said more than 4,000 people were evacuated in that district and a criminal case was opened over the dam's maintenance. Meduza reported the dam had been listed potentially hazardous since 2006, with only partial 2014 repairs, and that EMERCOM's republic-wide flood death figure was 6 while media tallies reached at least 7. Izvestia and Caucasian Knot said the Investigative Committee confirmed 4 deaths in Derbent District, including people in vehicles washed off the highway/canal after the dam burst. Prosecutors later said the operator had not ensured safe operation; company officials were detained or placed under house arrest.
incidents.status: Dam breached in April 2026; criminal investigation of operator officials ongoing as of mid-April reporting. Broader Dagestan flood emergency was described as stabilising by 7–9 April.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: More than 4,000 evacuated in Derbent District; Melikov said more than 6,200 people were affected by Dagestan floods overall
incidents.notes: deaths=4 is the Investigative Committee Derbent-district confirmation after the dam burst, not the higher republic-wide flood totals (6 official / 7–8 media). Incident day is 5 April in RIA; some later legal copy uses 6 April.
incidents.downstream_risk: Mamedkala and nearby settlements including Yuny Pakhar, Gejuk and Kala; more than 4,000 evacuated in Derbent District

incidents.name: Buck's Pond Dam
incidents.river_or_facility: Buck's Pond / Comstock Creek (to Hubbard Lake)
incidents.cause_summary: The dam failed amid rain-and-snowmelt flooding; EGLE later said stoplogs left in place reduced spillway capacity, after first stating the failure mechanism was not immediately clear.
incidents.what_happened: Michigan EGLE said it was notified on the night of 13 April 2026 that the privately owned, low-hazard Buck's Pond Dam near Barton City had failed amid northern Michigan rain-and-snowmelt flooding. Detroit News reporting republished by the USA TODAY Network said the ~94-year-old structure burst about 20:00, drained the pond, destroyed the gravel road over the dam, and sent water north down Comstock Creek toward Hubbard Lake. EGLE dam-safety chief Luke Trumble said downstream consequences appeared limited (trail, channel and floodplain) and that the failure mechanism was not immediately clear. Owner is the Lakes in the Green Association; last inventory inspection cited was August 2017, then rated satisfactory. In June 2026 EGLE issued a violation notice, saying stoplogs left in place reduced spillway capacity and citing several NREPA sections. No injuries were reported in the accounts fetched.
incidents.status: Dam failed and pond drained. EGLE violation notice issued by mid-June 2026; rebuild/funding unresolved in April owner comments.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Pond and local gravel road destroyed; no significant downstream life-safety threat per EGLE

sources.label: Detroit News via USA TODAY Network / Blue Water Healthy Living

incidents.notes: One of five April 2026 Michigan dam failures EGLE enumerated to MLive. Sister failures (Mavraganis; Atlanta campground; two Seney NWR embankments) lacked dedicated articles retrieved for full records.

incidents.name: Cement Lake Dam (Portland Reservoir)
incidents.location_label: West El Paso, Texas, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Cement Lake / Portland Reservoir (spring-fed; pump-down toward Rio Grande culverts)
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: engineers saw slow slope failures, embankment movement and seepage consistent with a possible breach before the dam was stabilised.
incidents.what_happened: El Paso Water, which acquired Cement Lake and about 300 acres from TxDOT in late March 2026, issued urgent updates on 23 April 2026 after engineers saw slow slope failures, slight embankment movement and seepage — indicators it said were consistent with a possible breach. Personnel were pulled to higher ground; USACE advisers were brought in; pumping began and roads including approaches toward Doniphan and Paisano were closed. EPWater said nearby homes sit on higher ground and were not expected to flood. KVIA's 26 April update quoted CEO John Balliew that crews had 'a very close call with a near-dam collapse' but had stabilised the dam and the risk was then 'very low' after as many as 16 pumps lowered the lake about 17 feet; earthwork on the compromised section resumed 25 April after being halted late on the 23rd when the section had 'already shown signs of breaching'. The lake area stayed closed to the public while long-term repairs were planned. No casualties were reported.
incidents.status: Stabilised as of 26 April 2026; roads reopened; lake area closed to the public; utility shifted from emergency response to a long-term repair plan. Not a completed breach.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: Road closures only; nearby homes not expected to be inundated (EPWater)

incidents.name: Dudhkumar river protection dyke (Muriarhat)
incidents.river_or_facility: Dudhkumar River protection dyke, Muriarhat / Adarshapara
incidents.cause_summary: Nearly 40 metres of river-protection dyke collapsed as the Dudhkumar ran 22 cm above its danger level, and floodwater entered villages through the gap.
incidents.what_happened: The Daily Star of 30 June 2026 reported that nearly 40 metres of Dudhkumar river-protection dyke collapsed late the previous night (29 June; a farmer quoted the paper said Monday night) at Muriarhat in Bamandanga union, Nageshwari, Kurigram, as the river ran 22 cm above its 29.60 m danger level at Pateshwari. BWDB executive engineer Rakibul Hasan said floodwater entered villages through the gap; the Bamandanga Union Parishad chairman said at least eight villages and about 5,000 families were stranded. A farmer said water entered around 250 households. BWDB prepared bamboo piling and sand-filled geobags. A 5 July Daily Star follow-up said water was receding and BWDB had started placing geobags on an unfinished 300-metre stretch of a 3,100-metre right-bank embankment delayed by land acquisition. No death toll for the dyke breach was given in those articles.
incidents.status: Temporary geobag closure reported by 5 July 2026; permanent completion of the remaining 300 m section planned after floodwater fully receded.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: About 5,000 families stranded in Bamandanga union (union chairman); ~250 households in Muriarhat (resident); wider Rangpur-region floods left more than 20,000 families stranded
incidents.notes: Monday 29 June 2026 is the incident night implied by the 30 June article and a resident quote. Regional 20,000-family figure is basin-wide flooding, not only this breach.
incidents.breach_size: nearly 40 metres of dyke collapsed
incidents.downstream_risk: at least eight villages and about 5,000 families stranded in Bamandanga union

incidents.name: Liulan (六蓝) Reservoir
incidents.region: Hengzhou, Nanning, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region
incidents.river_or_facility: Liulan Reservoir (Xiaoyi Town / Liulan village); discharge toward Yunbiao River / Yujiang
incidents.cause_summary: Typhoon Maysak rain caused Liulan Reservoir to overtop and breach on 6 July 2026.
incidents.what_happened: Typhoon Maysak rain caused Liulan Reservoir in Hengzhou to overtop and breach on 6 July 2026. Nanning raised flood-control emergency response to Level I; CCTV video showed a large release through the dam breach. At a 9 July news conference, Nanning Vice-Mayor Ding Wei said the Liulan breach had caused 26 deaths (5 then unidentified) and 7 people missing, while Guangxi overall had 39 dead and 9 missing — figures that could overlap pending DNA identification. Deputy water-resources director Zhai Jianjia said Liulan water had fallen below dam-foundation rock, the breach and discharge had largely stabilised, and crest access was restored that morning for dredging. Nanning reported 64,500 people evacuated or resettled by 11:00 on 9 July (54,500 in Hengzhou; 9,321 in Binyang).
incidents.status: Breach and downstream discharge reported largely stable as of 9 July 2026; search, identification, resettlement and a later State Council investigation were reported in subsequent Chinese coverage.

incidents.notes: Official 26 deaths is the Liulan-attributed figure from the 9 July Nanning briefing; regional Guangxi total was 39 dead / 9 missing and may overlap. Nearby Yunbiao (breach) and Liuwang (overtopping) are separate records.

incidents.downstream_risk: 64,500 evacuated/resettled across Nanning as of 9 July (54,500 Hengzhou)

incidents.region: Hengzhou, Nanning, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region
incidents.cause_summary: Nanning authorities said Yunbiao Reservoir overtopped and breached on 6 July 2026 in the same Typhoon Maysak episode as Liulan.

China Daily said Liulan and Yunbiao had reported overtopping and breaches since 6 July, threatening Xiaoyi and Yunbiao townships; Hengzhou's deputy mayor said water from the two reservoirs flows to the Yunbiao River then the Yujiang. incidents.name: Swift Creek Upper Reservoir
incidents.region: Afton / Swift Creek Canyon, Lincoln County, Wyoming
incidents.river_or_facility: Swift Creek Upper Reservoir (Lower Valley Energy hydro)
incidents.cause_summary: The sluice gate failed, causing an uncontrolled release; a camera inspection found catastrophic gate failure, destroyed panels and a broken operating rod.
incidents.what_happened: Lower Valley Energy said the sluice gate at Swift Creek Upper Reservoir failed in the early morning of 13 July 2026, causing an uncontrolled release that substantially drained the reservoir and carried sediment, trees and debris downstream (including material from a 2023 upstream landslide). Town of Afton staff told SVI the town water supply was not affected. CEO Bear Prairie later said a camera inspection found catastrophic gate failure, destroyed panels, and a broken operating rod; debris then partly plugged the opening and flows stabilised at a low reservoir level. LVE said the dam itself remains safe and is monitored. Permanent gate replacement requires FERC, U.S. Forest Service and other approvals, with at least a 60-day FERC review after the repair plan is submitted. The public was told to stay out of the reservoir bed and canyon.
incidents.status: Reservoir largely drained and held at a low level; dam reported safe and monitored; sluice-gate replacement plan in regulatory review as of late-July 2026 LVE/SVI updates. No deaths reported.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: No evacuation reported; public exclusion of reservoir and Swift Creek canyon

incidents.name: Ngawun River embankment (Laymyethna)
incidents.cause_summary: Heavy monsoon rain and riverbank erosion breached the Ngawun River embankment in Laymyethna Township.

incidents.name: Bagré Dam
incidents.region: Centre-Est / Bagré (downstream White Volta / northern Ghana on alert)
incidents.river_or_facility: Bagré Dam on the Nakambé / White Volta system
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: Ghana authorities monitored a possible controlled spill if rainfall pushed the reservoir to a stated threshold.
incidents.what_happened: Ghana's Water Resources Commission said on 4–5 August 2026 that SONABEL, operator of Burkina Faso's Bagré Dam, might begin a controlled spill from 11 August if the reservoir reached a critical level (WRC cited 232.93 m / 62.77% full on 4 August). NADMO later said SONABEL deferred the 11 August spill because upstream rainfall was lower than expected; as of that day the level was 233.08 m, 1.92 m below a 234.15 m threshold cited by NADMO. A Citi Newsroom report of SONABEL's 15 August update put Bagré at 233.24 m (77.35% full), 1.76 m below the 235 m normal reservoir level, and said SONABEL may open spillway gates if the level reaches 234.75 m, with public notice before any release. This is a seasonal controlled-spill watch, not a structural failure. Northern Ghana communities along the White Volta remained on alert.
incidents.status: No spill started as of the 15 August 2026 SONABEL figures reported by Citi Newsroom. Reservoir below stated spill thresholds; Ghana NADMO/WRC still monitoring.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: NADMO placed White Volta basin communities on alert (68 communities cited in Northern Region coverage); no flood from a 2026 Bagré spill reported in sources fetched
incidents.notes: Not a dam failure. Spill-threshold figures differ slightly across WRC, NADMO and the 15 August SONABEL update; all agree the dam had not spilled as of those reports.

incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (Balangir district; ~18 km downstream of Lower Suktel)

incidents.cause_summary: The newly built dam suffered cut-off-wall and downstream-embankment damage in early-August rains; the MLA’s letter said the sanctioned design had reduced waterway, gates and impervious floor.
incidents.what_happened: Newly built Chattamakhana Dam in Balangir district suffered damage in rains in early August 2026. incidents.name: Olde Mill Golf Club Dam
incidents.river_or_facility: Olde Mill Golf Resort lake / Stone Mountain Creek drainage toward Big Reed Island Creek
incidents.cause_summary: Intense rain was followed by failure of the primary spillway pipe; DCR said it had received none of the required owner documents since 2006 and the last emergency action plan expired in 2012.
incidents.what_happened: Intense rain on the night of 2 August 2026 flooded the Laurel Fork area of Carroll County. Virginia DCR Regional Engineer Steven Bricker observed on 4 August that the Olde Mill Golf Club lake (normal pool near 300 acre-feet) was almost completely drained after a partial breach. DCR's 5 August letter to owner Norris Mitchell / MG Golf Facilities LLC stated the primary spillway pipe failed, creating a scour hole around the riser and significant sediment loss; the dam has a preliminary high-hazard classification and may not impound water until corrective action. DCR said it had received none of the required owner documents since 2006 and the last emergency action plan expired in 2012. Owners were dewatering and beginning repairs as of mid-August; Carroll County said it issued no live alert because it learned of the flood after it ended.
incidents.status: Lake largely drained; DCR unsafe / non-imminent-danger notice in effect; dam not allowed to impound until corrective action; owner working on dewatering and spillway repair as of 18 August 2026.

incidents.name: Beiru River and Jialu River levee breaches
incidents.region: Henan (Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan; Chuanhui District, Zhoukou)
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (Jia County / Jiaxian; Beiru breach; Jialu at Zhoukou is separate)
incidents.cause_summary: Heavy rain from remnants of Typhoon Dolphin opened levee breaches on the Beiru and Jialu rivers.
incidents.what_happened: Heavy rain from remnants of Typhoon Dolphin opened a levee breach more than 40 metres wide on the Beiru River in Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan, on the night of Wednesday 12 August 2026; more than 2,000 people were relocated and Xinhua reported no casualties. That breach was sealed on Friday night 14 August after nearly two days of sandbagging, because heavy plant could not reach the narrow levee crown. A separate eastern-embankment breach on the Jialu River in Chuanhui District, Zhoukou, opened around 23:00 on Thursday 13 August, widening from about 30 metres to about 117 metres under Jialu inflows and Shaying River backwater. China Daily and People's Daily/Xinhua said the Jialu breach was sealed on Saturday night 15 August after more than 2,000 emergency personnel worked the site; crews continued raising, reinforcing and sealing seepage. A Level-IV national disaster-relief response was activated for Henan.
incidents.status: Both breaches reported sealed (Beiru 14 Aug; Jialu 15 Aug). Embankment raising, reinforcement and seepage control continuing at Jialu as of 15–16 August 2026.

incidents.what_happened: In a 14 August 2026 letter to the Lake Wynonah Property Owners Association, Kirk Kreider, acting chief of PADEP's Division of Dam Safety, declared the 1971 earthen Lake Wynonah Dam 'unsafe' and requested an immediate voluntary full drawdown of the 175-acre reservoir at up to one foot per day, with a formal order threatened if the association does not comply. The letter cited severe internal erosion, a crumbling concrete spillway, inability to pass a major flood, and temporary bracing of the top walls after a spillway collapse at the community's Fawn Lake Dam. Kreider wrote that 'unsafe' does not mean imminent failure, but that deficiencies could result in failure with loss of life or substantial property damage if not corrected. The lake had already been drawn down 10–15 feet in autumn 2025 after new seepage and a boil were reported. PADEP also said the high-hazard owner lacked required financial assurance.
